# Week 5 — The Interview Playbook

**Goal by Friday:** three timed 45-minute designs recorded and reviewed, with the
canonical problems answered from the pattern catalogue rather than from scratch.

**Why this module exists:** design ability and interview performance are different
skills. Plenty of engineers can build the right system and fail the interview anyway,
because they stayed silent, or never estimated, or narrated a diagram instead of defending
a decision.

---

## 1. Concepts (2 h)

### 1.1 The pattern catalogue

These patterns answer most canonical questions. Learn the *situation each one is for*, not
just the name.

| Pattern | Use it when | Cost / caveat |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Cache-aside** | Any read-heavy path | Staleness; stampede; cold start |
| **Read-through** | You want the cache to own loading | Hides the source of truth |
| **Write-behind** | Write latency dominates | **Data-loss window** |
| **Sharding** | One machine cannot hold the data or the writes | Cross-shard queries; re-sharding is painful |
| **Leader-follower** | Many reads, ordered writes | Replication lag; read-your-writes |
| **Multi-leader** | Multi-region writes | Conflict resolution; last-write-wins loses data |
| **Leaderless (quorum)** | Availability over strong consistency | You implement conflict resolution |
| **Event sourcing** | Audit trail / temporal queries required | Massive complexity; most systems do not need it |
| **CQRS** | Read and write models have very different shapes | Two models to keep in sync |
| **Saga** | A transaction spans services | Compensation, not rollback |
| **Outbox** | DB write + event publish must agree | Relay lag; duplicate delivery |
| **Idempotency key** | Any retryable non-idempotent operation | Retention window for keys |
| **Token bucket** | Rate limit with bursts allowed | Two knobs to tune |
| **Leaky bucket / token bucket at the edge** | Fairness per tenant | — |
| **Load shedding** | Overload protection | Users see errors (by design) |
| **Backpressure** | Consumer cannot keep up | Producer must slow or block |
| **Circuit breaker** | Dependency is failing | Cascading failure if mis-tuned |
| **Bulkhead** | Isolate resource pools per dependency | More pools, more memory |
| **Consistent hashing** | Many keys, high churn | Virtual nodes for balance |
| **Gossip protocol** | Membership / failure detection at scale | Eventual, probabilistic |
| **Anti-corruption layer** | Integrating a system you do not own | An extra service |
| **Sidecar** | Shared cross-cutting concerns (TLS, tracing) | More moving parts |
| **Blue/green** | Zero-downtime deploys | Double capacity during deploy |
| **Canary** | Limit blast radius of a change | Needs good metrics to judge |
| **Fan-out/fan-in** | Independent subtasks then aggregate | Aggregator is a bottleneck |
| **Side effect isolation** | Preventing cascading failure | Retries can amplify it |

**Why this is worth memorising:** when a question arrives, you are not inventing an
architecture, you are *selecting patterns and justifying them*. That is what a senior
engineer looks like.

### 1.2 The twelve canonical problems

| # | Problem | The shape of the answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Design URL shortener | Key generation, 25:1 read/write, cache, no sharding |
| 2 | Design a rate limiter | Token bucket, distributed store or local, per-tenant |
| 3 | Design a news feed | Fan-out on write, fan-in on read; hybrid for celebrities |
| 4 | Design WhatsApp/chat | WebSockets, presence, ordered messages, partitioning by conversation |
| 5 | Design a file storage (Dropbox) | Chunking, dedup by hash, CDN, signed URLs, metadata DB |
| 6 | Design a ticket booking site | **The consistency one.** Seat holds, saga, expiring reservations |
| 7 | Design an analytics pipeline | Ingest → queue → batch → OLAP store; late arrivals, dedup |
| 8 | Design a ride-sharing dispatcher | Matching, geo-indexing, supply/demand, surge pricing |
| 9 | Design a notification system | Priority queues, per-channel workers, retries, DLQ, dedup |
| 10 | Design a video transcoding pipeline | Job orchestration, DAGs, fan-out, storage tiers |
| 11 | Design a payment system | Ledger, idempotency, saga, reconciliation, no distributed txn |
| 12 | Design a CI/CD system | Webhook ingest, queue per job, isolation, artifact store |

**Notice what they have in common:** every one is decided by (a) the read/write ratio,
(b) the hardest single operation, and (c) the consistency requirement of the one thing
that matters. There is no mystery. There is pattern recognition plus arithmetic.

### 1.3 The questions that carry the most marks

| Signal | What it says about you |
| --- | --- |
| "I'll clarify scope first" | You do not build the wrong thing |
| "Assuming 2 writes per user per day…" | You reason with assumptions |
| "This is two terabytes, so we don't need to shard" | You can rule things out |
| "Read replicas, which means stale reads — fine here, not for balance" | You know trade-offs, not just options |
| "Let me go deep on the hardest part" | You prioritise |
| "If I split the queue by key, ordering holds per conversation" | You know where the guarantees end |
| "Here's how it fails and what I'd alert on" | You have operated things |
| "I don't know — I'd measure X" | Honest, and still useful |

**What loses marks:** jumping to a diagram, drawing six microservices when three suffice,
naming technologies without a reason, no numbers, and — the most common — going quiet.

### 1.4 Handling the scale questions

> *"Now design it for 10 million users."*

**Do not redesign from scratch.** Say this out loud:

> *"The shape stays; what changes is where the limits bind. At this scale reads no longer
> fit in one cache, so I add a CDN tier and shard the read path by user. The write path is
> the same. Let me talk through what breaks and what I'd do about each."*

**The checklist of what actually changes at 100×:**

| Limit | Symptom | Response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Single machine RAM | Cache/DB working set | Shard, tier storage |
| Single machine disk | Data volume | Shard by key, partition by time |
| Write throughput | Primary saturated | Shard writes, queue, batch |
| Read throughput | Primary CPU | Replicas + cache + CDN |
| Network bandwidth | Latency to users | CDN, compression, regional deployment |
| Single-region outage | Availability | Multi-AZ, then multi-region |
| Team size | Coordination | Modularity, then split services |

**The honest answer scores best:** *"At this scale I'd re-examine whether one database
still works. It probably does for storage, but I'd add replicas and a queue for writes."*
Interviewers are testing whether you can *reason about the change*, not whether you have
memorised 1M-user architectures.

### 1.5 Whiteboarding and the take-home

**Whiteboard rules:**
- Draw boxes and label **every** arrow with what flows and in which direction.
- Say the story out loud while you draw. Silence is the failure mode, not messy lines.
- Leave room to redraw. Cross things out; do not defend every stroke.
- If the interviewer corrects you, update immediately and thank them. That is a *good*
  signal — you are coachable.

**Take-home design review** — what they actually check:
- [ ] Requirements and explicit non-goals
- [ ] Estimates with assumptions stated
- [ ] Trade-offs *rejected*, with reasons
- [ ] Data model and consistency promise per feature
- [ ] Failure modes and the mitigation for each
- [ ] Observability: what you would measure and alert on
- [ ] Honest open questions

**What sinks a take-home:** a wall of technology with no reasoning, no numbers, no failure
analysis, and a diagram that would not survive a code review.

---

## 2. Lab — three timed designs (the week's main build)

### 2.1 Run them properly

| Round | Problems | Conditions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | URL shortener, rate limiter, chat | Untimed, 30 min each, reference notes allowed |
| 2 | Ticket booking, analytics pipeline, notifications | 45 min each, timed, notes allowed |
| 3 | News feed, file storage, payment system | 45 min each, **no notes**, recorded |

**Record the audio.** Listen back and score yourself against this rubric:

```
1  Clarified scope and asked questions first                 /5
2  Estimated scale with stated assumptions                  /5
3  Designed a data model with a consistency promise         /5
4  High-level architecture justified box by box             /5
5  Went deep on the two hardest parts                       /5
6  Named at least one rejected option and why              /5
7  Covered failure modes and degradation                    /5
8  Named metrics, alerts, and the 3am question              /5
-------------------------------------------------------------
   33+/40 to be interview-ready
```

### 2.2 The trap questions, and their answers

| Trap | The trap | The right answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "Use a microservices architecture" | Free pass to over-engineer | "I'll propose services along domain boundaries and start in a well-modularised monolith where the coupling is low — splitting is easier to justify once you can see the real traffic" |
| "How would you make it real-time?" | Temptation to add Kafka | "Push on write or a change-data-capture, keep reads on the request path, and stream only where the UX needs it" |
| "What if the database goes down?" | Assuming the cache saves you | "Writes stop and the cache serves stale reads. That's a deliberate availability trade — and the circuit breaker means we fail fast rather than queue" |
| "How would you scale to 1M users?" | Rewriting the design | "Same shape; the limits that bind move from CPU to storage and network. Here's what I'd add, in order" |
| "What database would you use?" | Technology shopping | "Relational, because we need transactions across these entities. I'd move to X only if this specific problem appeared" |
| "How do you handle failures?" | Vague answer | Name three: one dependency, one shard, one region — and the mitigation for each |

### 2.3 The "I don't know" protocol

Being wrong is fine. Being wrong *loudly and confidently* is what costs you.

> *"I don't know the exact answer for that piece. What I'd do is look at the query plan in
> production, and if it's a sequential scan on a large table, add a composite index on the
> equality and sort columns. That's my first move either way."*

That gets full credit. A confident invention gets zero.

---

## 3. Practical drills (2 h)

| # | Drill | Teaches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Re-answer 4 canonical problems from the pattern table only | Recognition replaces invention |
| 2 | Do a 15-min design with no architecture — requirements and data only | Depth over boxes |
| 3 | Hand a design to a colleague and defend it for 5 minutes | Finds the holes fast |
| 4 | Answer 10 "why not X" questions about your last design | Trade-off fluency |
| 5 | Watch a recorded interview and count unstated assumptions | Calibration |
| 6 | Design the same problem at 1k, 1M, 1B users | Scale reasoning is mechanical |

---

## 4. Deliverable — the interview dossier

- [ ] The 12 canonical problems, each answered in a one-page design
- [ ] Three timed 45-minute designs recorded and self-scored with the 40-point rubric
- [ ] A 2× improvement on the same rubric after the third round
- [ ] An error log: every question you could not answer, with the rule you now follow
- [ ] A written version of the 30-second project deep-dive (STAR: situation, task, action, result)
- [ ] Answers to the six trap questions, memorised

---

## 5. Self-check

1. You have 5 minutes and a blank whiteboard. What are your first three sentences?
2. Which pattern answers "the read is slow and the data never changes"?
3. You designed a chat system. Where is ordering guaranteed, and where is it not?
4. Give one design decision you would *reject* on a real system, and why.
5. The interviewer says your design is over-engineered. What do you say?
6. You cannot remember a specific API detail mid-interview. What is your sentence?

---

## 6. Cheat sheet

| Moment | Do |
| --- | --- |
| Start | Clarify scope, then estimate, then design |
| Estimate | State assumptions, round honestly, say what you do *not* need |
| Design | Boxes with labelled arrows; justify each one |
| Go deep | Pick the two hardest parts; name what you rejected |
| Scale question | Same shape; name which limit moved |
| Wrong | Update immediately, thank them |
| Don't know | Say so, describe how you'd find out |
| Finish | Failure modes, metrics, the 3am question |

# Projects & Capstone

You learn system design by building the mechanisms and watching them fail under load. Each
project below names the **one pattern it exists to teach**, so you can skip the ones you
already know and go deep on the ones you do not.

---

## Project 1 — URL shortener (Week 1)
**Teaches:** estimation, key generation, cache-aside, hot-key protection.

- [ ] Three short-code strategies compared and one chosen with reasoning
- [ ] `POST /urls` + `GET /{code}` with a 307 redirect
- [ ] Cache-aside with jittered TTL and single-flight
- [ ] Hot-key bypass for a viral code
- [ ] Load test: report throughput, p50/p95/p99, cache hit ratio

---

## Project 2 — Rate limiter (Week 3)
**Teaches:** token bucket, distributed state, fairness per tenant.

- [ ] Token bucket with configurable rate and burst
- [ ] Per-client **and** per-tenant limits, `429` with `Retry-After`
- [ ] Distributed version using a shared store, with a documented eventual-consistency gap
- [ ] Load test proving the limit holds under concurrency
- [ ] A write-up: why not a fixed window, and what the burst problem is

---

## Project 3 — News feed (Week 5)
**Teaches:** fan-out on write vs fan-in on read, the hybrid celebrity problem.

- [ ] Feed generation with pagination that does not drift
- [ ] Fan-out-on-read and fan-out-on-write, both implemented and benchmarked
- [ ] Hybrid: popular authors fanned out, the rest on read
- [ ] Documented staleness bound per strategy

---

## Project 4 — Chat service (Week 3)
**Teaches:** ordering, partitions, WebSockets, delivery guarantees.

- [ ] WebSocket connection handling with heartbeat and reconnect
- [ ] Messages partitioned by conversation id → **ordering within a partition**
- [ ] At-least-once delivery with a client-side dedupe on message id
- [ ] Presence, with an explicit documented accuracy trade-off
- [ ] A written statement of exactly which guarantees you do and do not provide

---

## Project 5 — File storage (Week 5)
**Teaches:** chunking, content-addressed dedup, CDN, signed URLs.

- [ ] Chunked upload with resumable sessions
- [ ] Dedup by content hash; prove the second upload stores no new bytes
- [ ] Metadata in a relational DB, bytes in object storage
- [ ] Signed, expiring download URLs
- [ ] Public files served entirely from a CDN with the origin unreachable in a test

---

## Project 6 — Ticket booking (Week 2) ← *the consistency one*
**Teaches:** the reservation saga, expiring holds, and why 2PC is wrong here.

- [ ] Seat inventory with a **hold** that expires after N minutes
- [ ] A saga: hold → payment → confirm, with compensations on each failure
- [ ] **No double-booking**, proven by a concurrency test hammering the last seat
- [ ] Payment failures release the hold; abandoned holds expire
- [ ] A written analysis of what happens if the payment provider succeeds and confirm fails

---

## Project 7 — Analytics pipeline (Week 5)
**Teaches:** late arrivals, dedup, rollups, a separate write path.

- [ ] Event ingest → queue → batch workers → a columnar/analytical store
- [ ] Client-generated event ids for dedup
- [ ] Handle late and out-of-order events; recompute affected windows
- [ ] Hourly and daily rollups so a dashboard query does not scan a year
- [ ] A dashboard query plan proving the rollups are used

---

## Project 8 — Notification system (Week 4)
**Teaches:** priority queues, per-channel workers, DLQ, deduplication, SLOs.

- [ ] Priority queue; low-priority work yields to high-priority work
- [ ] Per-channel workers (email, SMS, push) with independent scaling and rate limits
- [ ] Retry with capped jittered backoff, then DLQ
- [ ] User preferences and quiet hours
- [ ] SLIs per channel and a documented error-budget policy

---

## Project 9 — Video transcoding pipeline (Week 5)
**Teaches:** job DAGs, fan-out, storage tiers, idempotent workers.

- [ ] Upload triggers a DAG: probe → transcode ladder → thumbnails → publish
- [ ] Fan-out across workers with a queue per stage
- [ ] Each stage idempotent, so a worker crash and restart does not duplicate work
- [ ] Storage tiering: originals cold, derivatives hot
- [ ] Progress tracking and a failure report per stage

---

## Project 10 — Payment system (Week 2) ← *the hardest one*
**Teaches:** a ledger, idempotency, reconciliation, saga across providers.

- [ ] Double-entry ledger — every transaction is balanced or it is rejected
- [ ] Idempotency keys on every mutating endpoint
- [ ] Saga with compensations across auth, capture, and fulfilment
- [ ] **Nightly reconciliation** against the provider, with a report of discrepancies
- [ ] A test that fires the same request 10 times and asserts one charge

---

## Capstone — a system of your own

Pick a domain you understand from the inside (a marketplace, a booking system, a
collaboration tool, a delivery app) and design *and build* it to production standards.

**Required:**

- [ ] A full design document: requirements, estimates, API, data model, architecture, two
      deep dives, failure modes, metrics, open questions
- [ ] Every pattern in the catalogue that *applies* — and a written justification for every
      one that does not
- [ ] A consistency table: every feature, its promise, and the mechanism that enforces it
- [ ] A cache layer, a queue, and a rate limiter — each with a test that proves its
      behaviour under failure
- [ ] Idempotency on every mutating endpoint
- [ ] SLIs, SLOs, an error-budget policy, and a dashboard definition
- [ ] A chaos experiment with recorded results
- [ ] A load test report and a cost model
- [ ] A multi-region or DR decision, written down with reasoning
- [ ] A threat model covering tenant isolation and secrets

**Definition of done:**

- [ ] A 45-minute walkthrough of the system, recorded, that you would be happy to defend
- [ ] You can answer "why not X?" for every architectural choice
- [ ] You can name the three things you would change first, and why
- [ ] It is on GitHub with a README containing the design doc and the real numbers

---

## Portfolio polish (1 h)

1. **One line with a number:** *"Booking service, 5k peak rps, 99.95 % availability over 90
   days, zero double-bookings in a 10k-concurrent last-seat test."*
2. **ASCII architecture**, 10 lines, with the trade-off for each box inline.
3. **The numbers table** — throughput, percentiles, cost, and the SLO you actually hit.
4. **One chart that tells the story** — latency before/after the fix that mattered.
5. **"What I'd do next"** — three items, in priority order.
6. **A link to the design doc**, because that is the artefact being reviewed.

---

## The 30-minute project deep-dive (STAR)

Have this ready. It is asked in nearly every system design loop and it is the difference
between "I read about it" and "I did it".

| Part | What to say |
| --- | --- |
| **Situation** | The system, its scale, the constraint that hurt most |
| **Task** | The specific failure or requirement you owned |
| **Action** | Two or three decisions, each with the alternative you rejected |
| **Result** | A number, and one thing that is still unresolved |

Example shape:

> *"We were missing our 300 ms p99 on checkout. Reads were fine, so it was contention on
> the primary. We added a read replica — rejected, because checkout reads the freshly written
> cart, so staleness broke it — and instead moved seat holds to a serialisable transaction
> with a short hold timeout, plus an outbox so the confirmation event could not be lost. p99
> went from 780 ms to 190 ms and double-bookings went to zero under a 10k-concurrent test.
> The thing I would fix next is that the hold expiry sweep is still a cron job on one
> instance."*

That answer teaches: you measured, you rejected an option with a reason, you used the right
patterns, and you are honest about what remains.

---

## After the path: where to go next

| Direction | What to learn | Why it pays |
| --- | --- | --- |

# Java Developer — Start Here

**Who this is for.** Anyone who wants to write modern, production-grade Java — not a
Java-8 relic, and not a framework tour. This is the **language** path.

> **How this relates to the Spring Boot track.** They are companions, not duplicates.
> This track teaches the language, the runtime and the toolchain. The
> [`spring-boot-developer-path`](../spring-boot-developer-path) teaches the framework on
> top of them. If you are going to Spring, do this track first — you will understand every
> annotation, every lambda the framework hands you, and every stack trace far better.

---

## The version landscape (September 2026)

Java ships every six months. Every **even-numbered-then-LTS** pattern means: feature
releases in March and September, and an **LTS every two years**.

| Release | Date | Status | Use it? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Java 8 | Mar 2014 | EOL for Oracle updates | Only to maintain legacy systems |
| Java 11 | Sep 2018 | LTS, still in service | Legacy enterprise baseline |
| Java 17 | Sep 2021 | LTS, in service | Very common in production today |
| **Java 21** | Sep 2023 | LTS, in service | **Most common enterprise version right now** |
| **Java 25** | Sep 2025 | LTS, in service | **The target for this path** |
| Java 26 | Mar 2026 | Feature release, 6-month support | Skip; no reason to target it |
| **Java 27** | Sep 2026 | **Newest LTS** | Brand new — know what changed, don't deploy on day one |

**The professional recommendation:**

- **Write** code that compiles and runs on **Java 21+** — that is the widest compatibility
  window across the enterprise today.
- **Build and run on Java 25 LTS** — the mature current LTS, with the newest stable features
  and broad tool support.
- **Be aware of Java 27**, the newest LTS, and check the JEP list before adopting it. Two
  headline changes: **G1 becomes the default garbage collector in every environment**, and
  **post-quantum hybrid key exchange for TLS 1.3** enters the JDK.

> ⚠️ **Preview features are not features.** They change and can be removed between
> releases, and compiling with `--enable-preview` locks you to one JDK version. Use them to
> learn, never in production. The one exception people regret: none, so far.

---

## Where the modern features came from

You do not need to learn the old language first and then "upgrade". Learn it once, modern.

| Feature | Since | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lambdas & streams | 8 | Functional composition in the core language |
| `Optional` | 8 | Explicit absence — misused constantly, covered in Week 2 |
| Modules (`module-info.java`) | 9 | Real encapsulation at the jar boundary |
| `var` | 10 | Removes the type where it is already obvious |
| HTTP client | 11 | Replaces `HttpURLConnection` for real work |
| Switch expressions | 14 | No fall-through bugs, and they return values |
| Text blocks | 15 | Multi-line SQL, JSON, HTML in source |
| Records | 16 | Data carriers with `equals`/`hashCode`/`toString` for free |
| Pattern matching for `instanceof` | 16 | Removes the cast-after-check dance |
| Sealed types | 17 | Closed hierarchies the compiler can check exhaustively |
| Record patterns | 21 | Destructuring in `switch`, in one expression |
| Pattern matching for `switch` | 21 | Type *and* value dispatch, no visitor needed |
| **Virtual threads** | **21** | The biggest change to Java concurrency since 2004 |
| Sequenced collections | 21 | Ordered, deduplicated collection views |
| **Scoped values** | **25** | Safe, immutable per-task context — the ThreadLocal successor |
| Unnamed patterns/variables `_` | 21 (preview) | Explicitly ignoring a binding |

**One idea to carry through the whole track:** Java has been steadily adding *compile-time
safety over runtime introspection*. Sealed types, pattern matching and record patterns are
all the same movement — moving decisions from "check at runtime, hope" to "the compiler
proves it". Where you see a modern Java feature, ask what failure it makes impossible.

---

## The 7-week map

### Week 1 — Language core
Types and the type system, objects and immutability, records, sealed types, generics,
enums, `switch` expressions, pattern matching, `var`, text blocks, exceptions.
- **Lab:** a dependency-free `Money` / domain model using records, sealed types and
  exhaustive switches, with full JUnit coverage.
- **Why first:** everything else is built on this, and this is where the compiler starts
  working for you.

### Week 2 — Collections, streams and functional Java
`Collection` hierarchy and when to pick each, iteration, streams and the lazy pipeline,
`Collectors`, `Optional` done properly, functional error handling.
- **Lab:** a stream-based analytics pipeline over a large collection, with the complexity
  of each stage justified.
- **Why:** this is where Java code either becomes elegant or becomes unreadable.

### Week 3 — Concurrency and modern concurrency
Memory model, `synchronized` and locks, atomics, `CompletableFuture`, executors,
**virtual threads**, **structured concurrency** (preview), **scoped values** (25).
- **Lab:** a blocking-I/O service rewritten on virtual threads, with structured concurrency
  bounding the fan-out — and a measured throughput comparison.
- **Why:** the single largest change to how you write server code since Java 8.

### Week 4 — The modern standard library
`java.time`, `Optional` advanced, I/O and NIO, the HTTP client, text processing and
regular expressions, `RandomGenerator`, and the FFM API (preview) for off-heap memory.
- **Lab:** a file-processing pipeline using NIO, virtual threads, and structured concurrency.
- **Why:** most "I don't know Java well" complaints are really standard-library gaps.

### Week 5 — Build, test and toolchain
Maven and Gradle, dependency management, JUnit 5, AssertJ, Mockito, Testcontainers,
parameterised and nested tests, debugging, static analysis, code generation.
- **Lab:** a properly layered multi-module project with a real test pyramid.
- **Why:** the difference between code that works and code that can be changed safely.

### Week 6 — The JVM and performance
Memory model, object layout, the JIT, garbage collectors (G1, ZGC, Shenandoah), JFR,
`jcmd`/`jstack`/`jmap`, profiling, and tuning with evidence.
- **Lab:** take a deliberately slow service, profile it, fix it, and show the numbers.
- **Why:** "it is slow" becomes a measurement instead of a guess.

### Week 7 — Idioms, design and API craft
Null safety, immutability, error modelling, the design patterns worth using, domain
modelling, API design, backwards compatibility, module and package design, code review.
- **Lab:** refactor a procedural codebase into a modular, immutable, well-typed domain
  with a documented public API.
- **Why:** the last mile between working code and good code.

### Projects
See `projects.md` — six builds from a CLI to a high-throughput service, plus a capstone.

---

## Environment setup (first hour)

```bash
# Get a JDK 25 (LTS) — Temurin, Zulu, or Oracle, all fine
java -version          # expect 25.x
javac -version

# Build tool (use the wrapper, never a system Maven)
mvn -v                 # or: gradle -v
```

```bash
mkdir java-path && cd java-path
# Start from a single class, not a framework. Java needs no scaffolding.
cat > Hello.java <<'EOF'
public class Hello {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Start here: " + java.time.LocalDate.now());
    }
}
EOF
java Hello.java         # single-file source launcher, JDK 11+
```

**Tools worth installing in week one:**

| Tool | Why |
| --- | --- |
| IntelliJ IDEA (Community) | The best Java debugger and refactorer available |
| `sdk` (SDKMAN!) | Switch JDK versions per project without uninstalling |
| JShell | `jshell` in a terminal — experiment with APIs in seconds |
| VisualVM or JFR Viewer | Read what your program is actually doing |

**Use JShell constantly.** It is the fastest way to answer "what does this API actually
return?" without writing a file, compiling, or running anything.

---

## Working rhythm

| Block | Time | What you do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Read | 45 min | One module's concepts. Notes only. |
| Build | 2 h | The lab, from the spec. Compilable, tested. |
| Break | 30 min | Break it on purpose; read the actual stack trace. |
| Refactor | 30 min | Make it shorter and clearer. Measure the diff. |
| Commit | 15 min | With a message explaining *why*. |

**Rule:** your code must compile with **no warnings**. `-Xlint:all -Werror` in your build
turns style debt into a build failure, which is the only way it ever gets paid down.

---

## The habits that make you employable

1. **Prefer immutability.** `record` for data, `final` fields, no setters. Make illegal
   states unrepresentable.
2. **Constructor injection everywhere** — no field assignment after construction.
3. **Return types carry meaning.** Use `Optional<T>` deliberately, and understand exactly
   when *not* to.
4. **No raw types, no unchecked casts.** If you must cast, suppress with `@SuppressWarnings`
   and a comment explaining why it is safe.
5. **Test the behaviour, not the implementation.** A private method is tested through its
   public API.
6. **Read the stack trace.** All of it. The exception type, the message, and the frames.
   It is the fastest feedback loop you have.
7. **Know your bytecode target.** Set `--release 21` and never use an API newer than your
   declared target, or your build passes and production fails.

---

## How to use this platform

- The left rail is the curriculum, in order. Progress is stored in your browser.
- Every module ends with a **Lab**, **Deliverable**, and **Self-check**.
- The markdown in this folder is the source of truth — edit it, keep it as your notes.

# Week 5 — Build, Test & Toolchain

**Goal by Friday:** a multi-module project with a real test pyramid — fast unit tests,
slice tests, and Testcontainers integration tests against a real database — that builds
warning-free in CI.

**This is the module that separates code that works from code that can be changed safely.**

---

## 1. Concepts (3 h)

### 1.1 Maven — only what you need to know

```xml
<project>
  <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>
  <groupId>com.example</groupId>
  <artifactId>orders</artifactId>
  <version>1.0.0</version>

  <properties>
    <maven.compiler.release>21</maven.compiler.release>   <!-- NOT source/target -->
    <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
  </properties>

  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.junit.jupiter</groupId>
      <artifactId>junit-jupiter</artifactId>
      <version>5.11.0</version>
      <scope>test</scope>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>

  <build>
    <plugins>
      <plugin>
        <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
        <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
        <version>3.5.2</version>
      </plugin>
    </plugins>
  </build>
</project>
```

**`<release>21` over `<source>`/`<target>`.** This is the setting that matters most and the
one people get wrong: `source`/`target` only check the *language level*, so you can
compile against APIs from a newer JDK and get an `NoSuchMethodError` in production.
**`release` also validates the API surface.** If you say 21, the compiler will refuse to
let you call a method that only exists in 25.

**The dependency rules:**

| Rule | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **Never specify a version for a managed dependency** | That is how CVE-ridden transitive trees start |
| **Never use `system` scope** | It breaks reproducibility and security |
| **Run `mvn dependency:tree` before adding anything** | Often you already have it transitively |
| **Spring Boot: use the parent or the BOM** | The parent manages versions for the whole ecosystem |

```bash
./mvnw clean verify           # compile + test + package
./mvnw -Dtest=OrderTest test  # one class
./mvnw -Dgroups=slow test     # a tagged subset
./mvnw -Pprod package         # a profile
./mvnw dependency:tree        # what is actually on my classpath
```

**Always use the wrapper** (`./mvnw`), committed to the repo. It pins the Maven version, so
every developer and CI runs the same one.

### 1.2 Gradle — worth knowing, not worth arguing about

```kotlin
plugins {
    java
    id("org.springframework.boot") version "3.5.0"
}

java { toolchain { languageVersion = JavaLanguageVersion.of(21) } }

dependencies {
    testImplementation(platform("org.junit:junit-bom:5.11.0"))
    testImplementation("org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter")
}

tasks.test { useJUnitPlatform() }
```

**The one thing to know about Gradle:** the **build cache** and **configuration cache**.
A correct, incrementally-built Gradle build is dramatically faster than Maven on a large
project — which is why most new Java projects use it. The trade-off is a real learning
curve and a much larger error surface.

**Practical stance:** learn to *use* Gradle, understand dependency management and the
task graph, and let the team choose. Both are legitimate; a team that mixes both is the
actual problem.

### 1.3 JUnit 5 — the parts that matter

```java
class OrderServiceTest {

    private final OrderRepository repo = new InMemoryOrderRepository();
    private final OrderService service = new OrderService(repo, new PricingService(),
            () -> Instant.parse("2026-01-01T00:00:00Z"));   // injected clock = deterministic

    @Test
    @DisplayName("assigns sequential ids")
    void assignsSequentialIds() {
        assertThat(service.place("SKU-1", 1).id()).isEqualTo(1);
        assertThat(service.place("SKU-2", 1).id()).isEqualTo(2);
    }

    @Nested
    @DisplayName("when stock is insufficient")
    class InsufficientStock {

        @Test
        @DisplayName("rejects the order")
        void rejects() {
            assertThatThrownBy(() -> service.place("SKU-1", 99))
                    .isInstanceOf(InsufficientStockException.class)
                    .hasMessageContaining("SKU-1");
        }

        @BeforeEach
        void setUp() { repo.save(product("SKU-1", stock = 1)); }
    }
}
```

**`@Nested` classes are the most underused JUnit 5 feature.** They give you
`place → when stock is insufficient → rejects the order` naming, shared setup per
condition, and no giant single test class.

| Feature | Use it for |
| --- | --- |
| `@Nested` | Grouping by scenario, with per-group setup |
| `@ParameterizedTest` + `@CsvSource` | The same logic across many inputs |
| `@MethodSource` | Inputs generated by a method — great for edge cases |
| `@RepeatedTest` | Detecting flakiness from hidden state |
| `@Timeout` | Guarding against a hanging test |
| `@TestMethodOrder` | **Avoid** — it means your tests are not independent |
| `@Disabled` | Temporary only, with a reason and an issue link |

```java
@ParameterizedTest
@CsvSource({
        "'',            false",
        "'2026-13-01',  false",
        "'2026-02-30',  false",     // reject invalid dates
        "'2026-03-01',  true",
})
@DisplayName("validates ISO dates")
void validatesIsoDates(String input, boolean expected) {
    assertThat(validator.isValidDate(input)).isEqualTo(expected);
}

@ParameterizedTest
@MethodSource("edgeCaseAmounts")
void handlesEdgeCaseAmounts(BigDecimal amount) {
    assertThatNoException().isThrownBy(() -> new Money(amount, USD));
}

static Stream<BigDecimal> edgeCaseAmounts() {
    return Stream.of(BigDecimal.ZERO, new BigDecimal("0.01"),
            new BigDecimal("999999999.99"), new BigDecimal("1E+3"));
}
```

### 1.4 AssertJ — assertions you can read

```java
assertThat(result)
    .isNotNull()
    .extracting(Order::status, Order::total)
    .containsExactly(Status.SHIPPED, new BigDecimal("42.50"));

assertThat(list)
    .hasSize(3)
    .allSatisfy(o -> assertThat(o.total()).isPositive())
    .extracting(Order::id)
    .doesNotHaveDuplicates();

assertThatThrownBy(() -> service.place(id))
    .isInstanceOf(InsufficientStockException.class)
    .hasMessageContaining("SKU-1")
    .hasNoCause();               // or .hasCauseInstanceOf(...) when you care
```

**`assertThat` with a descriptive message, not `assertTrue(x != null)`.** When a test fails
at 2am, the assertion *is* your documentation.

### 1.5 Mocking — and its limits

```java
@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class OrderServiceTest {

    @Mock PaymentGateway gateway;
    @InjectMocks OrderService service;      // constructor injection -> clean wiring

    @Test
    void chargesOnConfirmation() {
        when(gateway.charge(anyString(), eq(4250))).thenReturn(Receipt.ok("tx-1"));

        var order = service.confirm("ORD-1");

        verify(gateway).charge("ORD-1", 4250);           // verify the interaction
        assertThat(order.status()).isEqualTo(Status.PAID);
    }

    @Test
    void doesNotChargeWhenAlreadyPaid() {
        var order = service.load("ORD-1").markPaid();
        service.confirm(order);
        verifyNoInteractions(gateway);                   // a real assertion, not a default
    }
}
```

**Where mocks are appropriate:** external services, the network, the clock, randomness.
**Where they are not:** your own domain logic. Mocking your own classes means testing
nothing but your assumptions.

**Three techniques worth knowing:**

```java
when(gateway.charge(any(), any())).thenReturn(Receipt.ok("1"))
                                   .thenReturn(Receipt.ok("2"));   // sequential returns
when(repo.findById(anyString())).thenAnswer(i -> Optional.of(order(i.getArgument(0))));
verify(gateway, times(3)).charge(any(), any());
verify(gateway, never()).refund(any(), any());
```

### 1.6 Testcontainers — integration tests that tell the truth

An in-memory database proves nothing about your real SQL. Testcontainers runs the real
thing.

```java
@SpringBootTest
@Testcontainers
class OrderRepositoryIT {

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection                     // Boot 3.1+: wires URL and credentials for you
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> db = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");

    @Autowired OrderRepository repo;
    @Autowired JdbcTemplate jdbc;

    @Test
    void respectsThePartialUniqueIndex() {
        repo.save(order("ORD-1"));
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> repo.saveAndFlush(order("ORD-1")))
                .isInstanceOf(DataIntegrityViolationException.class);
    }

    @Test
    void usesTheIndexWeDesigned() {
        var plan = explain("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC");
        assertThat(plan).contains("Index Scan");        // not Seq Scan on a big table
    }
}
```

**Why this is worth the extra seconds:** the tests that only fail against real PostgreSQL
are collation behaviour, index usage, constraint names, timestamp precision, transaction
isolation, and `NULL` semantics. Every one of them has bitten a team that tested on H2.

### 1.7 Static analysis, and the build that fails on a warning

| Tool | Catches | Effort |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `-Xlint:all -Werror` | Compiler warnings | Free — do it today |
| **SpotBugs** | Null dereferences, resource leaks, bad locking | Low config, high value |
| **Error Prone** | Bugs the compiler misses, at compile time | Low config, some false positives |
| Checkstyle / PMD | Style and complexity rules | Low value; keep the config tiny |
| **JaCoCo** | Coverage, with a diff-aware gate | Low |

```xml
<plugin>
  <groupId>com.github.spotbugs</groupId>
  <artifactId>spotbugs-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>4.9.3.0</version>
</plugin>

<!-- JaCoCo: fail the build if coverage DROPS, not for an absolute number -->
<rule>
  <element>BUNDLE</element>
  <limits>
    <limit>
      <counter>LINE</counter>
      <value>COVEREDRATIO</value>
      <minimum>0.70</minimum>
    </limit>
  </limits>
</rule>
```

**Coverage is a diagnostic, not a target.** 100 % coverage with no meaningful assertions is
worse than 60 % with good ones. Gate on *regression* — coverage must not go down — rather
than chasing a number.

### 1.8 Debugging like an adult

1. **Read the whole stack trace.** The exception type, the message, and *every* frame. The
   cause is usually at the bottom.
2. **Reproduce it in a test** before you fix it. A bug you cannot reproduce is a bug you
   cannot verify you fixed.
3. **Conditional breakpoints** in the IDE, and a watch expression for the state you care
   about.
4. **JFR for anything timing-related** — it is low overhead and runs in production.
5. **Learn to read a heap dump** — at least the dominator tree and one leak pattern.

---

## 2. Lab — a multi-module project (the week's main build)

```
parent/                    pom.xml, dependency management, plugin config
├── domain/                records, sealed types, domain exceptions — NO dependencies
├── service/               business logic, depends on domain
└── adapter-persistence/   Spring Data, Flyway, depends on domain
```

### 2.1 A real test pyramid

```java
// Layer 1 — pure unit, no Spring, milliseconds
class MoneyTest {
    @Test void refusesCurrencyMixing() { /* ... */ }
}

// Layer 2 — slice, one framework concern, sub-second
@DataJpaTest
class OrderRepositoryTest { /* real DB via Testcontainers, no service layer */ }

// Layer 3 — full integration, the slow ones, tagged
@SpringBootTest
@Tag("slow")
class CheckoutFlowIT { /* the whole wiring, real Postgres */ }
```

**The build must be honest about the cost:**

```xml
<plugin>
  <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
  <configuration>
    <groups>!slow</groups>          <!-- the default run skips integration tests -->
  </configuration>
  <executions>
    <execution>
      <id>integration</id>
      <phase>verify</phase>
      <goals><goal>integration-test</goal></goals>
      <configuration><groups>slow</groups></configuration>
    </execution>
  </executions>
</plugin>
```

### 2.2 Module boundaries, enforced

```java
// domain must not depend on anything — including the framework
@Test
void domainHasNoFrameworkDependencies() throws IOException {
    try (var files = Files.walk(Path.of("target/classes"))) {
        files.filter(f -> f.toString().endsWith(".class"))
             .forEach(f -> assertThat(readClassName(f))
                     .doesNotStartWith("org.springframework")
                     .doesNotStartWith("jakarta."));
    }
}
```

**An ArchUnit test is the better version of this** and takes five minutes:

```java
@Test
void servicesMustNotDependOnAdapters() {
    noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..service..")
        .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAnyPackage("..adapter..", "org.springframework.web..")
        .check(new ClassFileImporter().importPackages("com.example"));
}
```

### 2.3 Measure the build

```bash
time ./mvnw clean verify
./mvnw -Dtest='*Test' test     # unit only
```

Record: unit suite time, integration suite time, and the total. **If your full test suite
is over two minutes, developers will start skipping it, and a skipped suite is a broken
safety net.** The fix is tagging and splitting, not patience.

---

## 3. Practical drills (2 h)

| # | Drill | Teaches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Compile with `source/target` and call a newer API; then with `release` | The setting that prevents production failures |
| 2 | Break a test into `@Nested` groups | Readable failure names |
| 3 | Parameterise 5 tests into 1 | Table-driven tests |
| 4 | Find a real bug in a test suite by running it 20 times | Flakiness is usually shared state |
| 5 | Run SpotBugs; fix the top 3 findings | Static analysis finds real bugs |
| 6 | Time the suite; tag the slow tests | Making the fast path fast |
| 7 | Write an ArchUnit boundary test | Enforcing architecture, not documenting it |

---

## 4. Deliverable — the multi-module project

- [ ] Parent + 3 modules, with `mvnw` committed and `release` (not source/target) set
- [ ] A domain module with **zero** framework dependencies, and a test proving it
- [ ] Unit tests with no Spring context; slice tests; Testcontainers integration tests
- [ ] `@Nested` scenario grouping and ≥ 3 `@ParameterizedTest`s
- [ ] Slow tests tagged and excluded from the default run
- [ ] `mvn clean verify` green, SpotBugs clean, `-Xlint:all -Werror` enforced
- [ ] An ArchUnit test for the module boundaries
- [ ] A measured build time table, with a note on what you would move to a faster tier
- [ ] `README.md` with the build commands, the test strategy, and the timings

---

## 5. Self-check

1. What does `--release 21` catch that `source`/`target` does not?
2. When is a mock the wrong tool?
3. Why is an in-memory database worse than no test?
4. What is `@Nested` for, beyond organisation?
5. Your full suite takes 4 minutes. What happens to the team, and what do you do?
6. Name two bugs Testcontainers catches that H2 never will.

---

## 6. Cheat sheet

| Need | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Correct language + API level | `<release>` / `toolchain` |
| Deterministic tests | Inject `Clock` and `RandomGenerator` |
| Many inputs, one assertion | `@ParameterizedTest` + `@CsvSource` |
| Scenario grouping | `@Nested` |
| Readable assertions | AssertJ `assertThat` with extractors |
| External boundary | Mockito |
| Real database | Testcontainers + `@ServiceConnection` |
| Find latent bugs | SpotBugs, Error Prone, `-Xlint:all -Werror` |
| Enforce architecture | ArchUnit |
| Keep coverage honest | JaCoCo diff gate |
| Debug a timing issue | JFR, not `System.out` |

# Week 6 — The JVM & Performance

**Goal by Friday:** you have taken a deliberately slow service, found the bottleneck with
a profiler, fixed it, and can show the before/after numbers with the GC and allocation data
to back it up.

**The rule for this whole module: never guess. Measure, then change one thing, then measure
again.** Guessing at performance is how teams spend a month making something 4 % faster.

---

## 1. Concepts (3.5 h)

### 1.1 Memory layout — why object size matters

A Java object on a 64-bit HotSpot JVM with compressed oops (the default under 32 GB heap):

```
Object header  12 bytes  (mark word 8 + klass pointer 4, compressed)
Fields        4 or 8 bytes each, with padding
```

```java
// Three fields, three different sizes
class A { int x; }                    // 12 + 4 → padded to 16 bytes
class B { long x; }                   // 12 + 8 → 24 bytes (alignment)
class C { long x; long y; }           // 12 + 16 → 32 bytes
class D { Object o; }                 // 12 + 4 → 16 bytes
```

**The consequences that actually bite:**

| Consequence | Why |
| --- | --- |
| **A million small objects is a lot of memory** | Object overhead dominates; a `List<Small>` of 1M entries can be hundreds of MB of *headers* |
| **Padding wastes space** | Field order does not matter to the JVM, but alignment does |
| **Larger `-XX:MaxHeapSize` disables compressed oops** | Above ~32 GB, references become 8 bytes and your heap effectively grows — a classic production surprise |
| **Value objects beat `Integer`/`Long` in lists** | `List<Integer>` boxes every element; a primitive-specialised list does not |

```java
// Boxing is the usual hidden allocation in "fast" code
List<Integer> ids = new ArrayList<>();      // an Integer object per element
int[] primitiveIds = new int[1_000];        // 4 KB total, no objects at all
```

**Escape analysis** is the JVM's counter-move: if an object does not escape a method, the
compiler can eliminate the allocation entirely. It works for small, local, non-escaping
objects — which is exactly what records and small immutable value types are good for.

### 1.2 The JIT — why Java is fast, and when it is not

```
Interpreted  →  C1 (fast compile, basic opts)  →  C2 (slow compile, aggressive opts)
   slow            medium                                fastest
```

| Concept | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Tiered compilation** | The default: C1 for hot-enough methods, C2 for very hot ones |
| **Profile-guided optimisation** | The JIT counts which branches actually run and specialises for them |
| **Deoptimisation** | The JIT assumed something, got it wrong, and decompiles back to the interpreter |
| **Escape analysis** | Stack-allocate or eliminate non-escaping objects |
| **Inlining** | The single most important optimisation; only small methods get inlined |
| **OSR** | On-stack replacement — switch a running loop to compiled code mid-execution |

**The practical consequences:**

1. **Benchmark with a warm-up.** The first few thousand iterations measure the interpreter.
   Always discard warm-up iterations.
2. **Megamorphic call sites kill performance.** If a call site sees 50 different
   implementation types, the JIT can no longer inline it. This is why a
   `List<Object>`-typed structure is a hidden performance cliff.
3. **`final` on classes helps the JIT** by removing a subclass from the type profile.
4. **"Write boring, predictable code" is a real performance strategy.** Branchy,
   polymorphic code defeats the optimiser even when it is algorithmically fine.

### 1.3 Garbage collection — the collectors you must know

| Collector | Model | Best for | Pause behaviour |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **G1** | Region-based, generational | General-purpose, the sensible default | ~10–100 ms targets, adjustable pause goal |
| **ZGC** | Concurrent, generational | Very large heaps, strict low-latency | Sub-millisecond pauses |
| **Shenandoah** | Concurrent | Low latency on modest hardware | Sub-millisecond |
| Parallel | Stop-the-world, throughput | Batch jobs, short-lived processes | Longest pauses, best throughput |
| Epsilon | No collection at all | Testing, benchmarking, short jobs | You run out of memory |

**Java 27 (JEP 523) makes G1 the default garbage collector in every environment**, and Java
26 improved G1 plus added AOT caching that works with any collector. **If you deploy on 21
or 25, G1 is already the default on server-class machines** — the change makes 27
consistent everywhere. The point for you: **G1 is the collector you will actually run.**

```bash
# The five flags that cover almost every case
-XX:+UseG1GC
-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0            # size the heap from the container limit
-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError         # fail fast, do not limp
-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError     # get evidence before the crash
-XX:StartFlightRecording=filename=app.jfr,settings=profile
```

**`MaxRAMPercentage` is the single most important container flag.** Without it the JVM sizes
its heap from the *host's* RAM, not the container's limit, and the process gets
OOM-killed by the kernel while the JVM still thinks it has memory. This is the most common
container bug in Java, and it is entirely avoidable.

**What the collectors cannot fix:** a leak is a leak. G1, ZGC and Shenandoah are all
garbage *collectors*, not garbage *disablers*. A static map holding every request ever
processed is retained under every collector.

### 1.4 Reading the GC logs

```bash
# Turn on unified GC logging and analyse it
java -Xlog:gc*,safepoint:file=gc.log:time,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20M -jar app.jar
```

What to look for:

| Signal | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Pause frequency and duration | Above your latency SLO? G1 is missing its pause goal |
| Promotion rate | Objects surviving two collections — usually an allocation-rate problem |
| Allocation failure / `to-space exhausted` | Full GC, then a very long pause |
| Humongous allocations | Large arrays bypassing the normal path — a G1-specific problem |
| Pause time growing with heap | Either a leak, or a survivor space that is too small |

**Do not tune blind.** Change one flag, produce comparable logs, and compare. A GC tuning
exercise without before/after data is folklore.

### 1.5 JFR — the profiler that runs everywhere

```bash
java -XX:StartFlightRecording=duration=60s,filename=app.jfr,settings=profile -jar app.jar
# or attach to a running process
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=diag settings=profile duration=60s filename=diag.jfr
```

**Low overhead (1–2 %), production-safe, and it answers nearly every performance question:**

| JFR event type | Answers |
| --- | --- |
| `jdk.ObjectAllocationSample` | Which code is allocating the most? |
| `jdk.CPULoad` / ExecutionSample | Where is the CPU going? |
| `jdk.JavaMonitorEnter` | Where is lock contention? |
| `jdk.GarbageCollection` | Pause times and cause |
| `jdk.ThreadPark` | Where are threads blocking? |
| `jdk.SocketRead` | Time waiting on the network |
| `jdk.FileRead` / `FileWrite` | Time in file I/O |

**The question to answer with JFR is always one of: CPU, allocation, lock contention, or
waiting.** Four categories, and JFR will point at the right one in five minutes.

### 1.6 Diagnostics: `jcmd`, `jstack`, `jmap`, `jstat`

```bash
jcmd <pid> Thread.print                  # same as jstack — where are threads stuck?
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info                 # heap usage per generation
jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/heap.hprof # take a heap dump
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=diag duration=60s
jstat -gc <pid> 1000                    # GC counters every second
```

**Reading a thread dump — the pattern to look for:**

```
"http-nio-8080-exec-7"  #31  prio=5  BLOCKED
   java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object monitor)
     at com.example.Inventory.reserve(Inventory.java:42)      <-- THE LOCK
   - waiting to lock <0x00000000f1a2b3c0>                      <-- what it wants
     (a com.example.Inventory)
   - locked <0x00000000d4e5f6a0>                                <-- what it holds
     (a com.example.Connection)
```

**"BLOCKED, holding a lock, waiting for another" across two threads in a cycle is a
deadlock** — and the JVM prints `Found one Java-level deadlock` when it detects one. The
pair of conflicting frames is your entire diagnosis.

**A heap dump is the tool for leaks.** Load it into VisualVM or MAT and look at the
**dominator tree**: the objects that, if freed, would free the most memory. A
`static Map` retaining every request is obvious there and invisible everywhere else.

---

## 2. Lab — profile and fix a slow service (the week's main build)

**Spec:** a deliberately inefficient service. Find the bottleneck with evidence, fix it,
and report before/after with GC data.

### 2.1 The instrumentation you need first

```java
@Timed(value = "app.order.checkout", percentiles = {0.5, 0.95, 0.99})
public CheckoutResult checkout(Order order) { ... }

@Timed(value = "app.db.query", percentiles = {0.99})
@Counted
public List<LineItem> findLines(String orderId) { ... }
```

Percentiles, not averages: **an average latency hides exactly the users who are having a
bad time.** A p50 of 20 ms with a p99 of 2,000 ms is not a 20 ms service.

### 2.2 The measurement harness

```java
record Bench(String label, long p50Micros, long p99Micros, long allocationsPerOp) {}

static Bench measure(String label, Runnable task, int iterations, int warmup) {
    for (int i = 0; i < warmup; i++) task.run();          // JIT warm-up, discarded

    var samples = new long[iterations];
    for (int i = 0; i < iterations; i++) {
        long start = System.nanoTime();
        task.run();
        samples[i] = System.nanoTime() - start;
    }
    Arrays.sort(samples);
    return new Bench(label,
            TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS.toMicros(samples[(int) (iterations * 0.50)]),
            TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS.toMicros(samples[(int) (iterations * 0.99)]),
            0);   // allocation count comes from JFR
}
```

### 2.3 The hunt — in this order

```bash
# 1. CPU or waiting? 30 seconds of data settles it
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=diag settings=profile duration=30s filename=diag.jfr

# 2. Check GC first — it is the cheapest thing to rule out
jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000
#   If O (old gen) climbs and never comes down -> that is a leak, stop and find it.
#   If pause times are high -> allocation rate or heap sizing, before anything else.

# 3. Take a thread dump while it is slow
jcmd <pid> Thread.print > threads.txt
#   BLOCKED threads -> lock contention. RUNNABLE in the same method -> CPU.
#   WAITING with a socket -> the network.
```

### 2.4 The three classic fixes, and what each should move

| Finding | Fix | Should move |
| --- | --- | --- |
| High allocation in a loop | Reuse objects, avoid boxing, primitives over wrappers | GC time, throughput |
| Lock contention on a shared counter | `LongAdder` over `AtomicLong` | p99, dramatically |
| A slow call dominated by waiting | Virtual threads (Week 3) or caching | p99, dramatically |
| `Sequential Scan` on a large table | The right composite index | DB time |
| The heap growing without bound | Static state; find it in the dominator tree | Everything, eventually |

**Record the result honestly.** If the fix bought 15 %, say 15 % and explain why you
expected more — that is a far better engineering artefact than a number you are not sure
about.

---

## 3. Practical drills (2 h)

| # | Drill | Teaches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Run a container with no `MaxRAMPercentage` and a 512 MB limit; watch it die | The most common Java container bug |
| 2 | Benchmark with and without a warm-up loop | Measuring the interpreter otherwise |
| 3 | Compare `AtomicLong` vs `LongAdder` under 32 threads | Contention costs p99 |
| 4 | Fill a static `Map`; watch the heap climb; find it in a heap dump | Leaks defeat every collector |
| 5 | Take a JFR recording of a busy service; find the top allocation site | Four questions, one tool |
| 6 | Produce a deadlock with two locks; read the JVM's deadlock report | Thread dumps are readable |
| 7 | Force a Full GC; read `jstat` output and interpret each column | The numbers mean something |

---

## 4. Deliverable — the profiled service

- [ ] A deliberately slow service, committed **before** the fix, so the diff is the story
- [ ] p50 / p95 / p99 instrumentation, with percentiles not averages
- [ ] A JFR recording of the slow version and the fast version
- [ ] GC logs for both, with the allocation rate and pause times compared
- [ ] A written diagnosis: CPU, allocation, contention, or waiting — with evidence
- [ ] Exactly one change at a time, each with its own before/after measurement
- [ ] Final `jcmd` flags documented, including `MaxRAMPercentage` and OOM handling
- [ ] A README table: metric, before, after, and the explanation for the gap

---

## 5. Self-check

1. What does `--release` protect against that a JFR recording cannot?
2. Why does a container without `MaxRAMPercentage` get OOM-killed?
3. Your p50 is 20 ms. Your users still complain. Which percentile do you check, and why?
4. What are the four questions JFR is designed to answer?
5. `AtomicLong` vs `LongAdder` — which, and under what contention?
6. G1, ZGC, Shenandoah: which fixes a memory leak?

---

## 6. Cheat sheet

| Symptom | Look at |
| --- | --- |
| Container OOM-killed | `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage`, container limits |
| p99 bad, p50 fine | JFR `ThreadPark` / `SocketRead` — waiting |
| CPU at 100 % | JFR `ExecutionSample` |
| Frequent young GCs | Allocation rate, not a leak |
| Old gen never drops | A leak — dominator tree in a heap dump |
| Threads BLOCKED | `jcmd Thread.print` — lock contention |
| High p99 on counters | `LongAdder` |
| Long GC pauses | JFR `GarbageCollection` events |
| Everything is slow, nothing specific | Warm-up — measure again after JIT |

**Definition of done:** a colleague can clone it and run `./mvnw verify` and `./mvnw

thirty minutes.

## Portfolio polish (1 h)

1. **One line with a number:** *"Inventory service: 12k req/s, p99 4 ms, 3,000 virtual
   threads, 41 MB/op allocation, profiled with JFR."*
2. **ASCII architecture** — 10 lines, with the module rule stated inline.
3. **The load-test table**, including p99 and GC pauses. Anyone can claim throughput;
   p99 plus pauses is evidence.
4. **The JFR before/after** for one real fix.
5. **"What I'd do next"** — three items, ordered.
6. **A link to the ADRs**, because that is the artefact a reviewer most wants to read.

## The 30-minute project deep-dive (STAR)

| Part | What to say |
| --- | --- |
| **Situation** | The service, its scale, the constraint that hurt most |
| **Task** | The specific problem you owned |
| **Action** | Two or three decisions, each with what you rejected |
| **Result** | A number, and one thing still unresolved |

Example shape:

> *"We had p99 of 800 ms on checkout and the pool was exhausted at 200 threads. I profiled
> it with JFR rather than guessing: 70 % of the time was thread parking on socket reads, not
> CPU — so it was a concurrency-model problem, not a slow query. We moved the blocking
> client onto virtual threads with a semaphore bound of 64. I rejected going reactive
> because the codebase was synchronous and the correctness risk was higher than the gain.
> p99 went to 40 ms and we now run 3,000 concurrent requests on 8 cores. The thing I'd fix
> next is that the semaphore is a hand-tuned constant with no autoscaling."*

That answer demonstrates: you measured, you chose based on evidence, you rejected an
option with a reason, and you are honest about what remains.
